newsitem.title: USA: House Democrats seek U.S. nuclear waste bill delay.
newsitem.headline: House Democrats seek U.S. nuclear waste bill delay.

text.p: Four Democrats urged House energy and power subcommittee chairman Dan Schaefer to delay voting on a bill that calls for building a temporary dump in Nevada for spent fuel from nuclear plants, according to a letter released Wednesday.
Schaefer's spokeswoman said he had not responded to the July 29 letter.
Schaefer, a Colorado Republican, scheduled a vote for Thursday on the bill, which is being pushed by the nuclear industry and opposed by the Clinton administration.
The four Democrats, led by Rep. Ed Markey of Massachusetts, said the panel should not rush into debating the bill because lawmakers had held only one hearing on it this year.

"We believe that such an important piece of legislation, which would dramatically change the rules governing the transportation, interim storage, and permanent disposal of the nation's high-level radioactive waste, merits further examination before the Subcommittee proceeds to a markup," the Democrats, who are all on the House Commerce Committee, said.
"We would therefore strongly urge you to consider delaying a markup of this legislation," their letter said.

Earlier this month, House Commerce Committee chairman Thomas Bliley, a Virginia Republican, said he did not plan to move on the legislation until at least September, because he wanted to be sure there were enough votes in the House to override an expected White House veto.

He said he was also waiting to see how a court ruled in a lawsuit filed by utilities and states seeking to stop the government from collecting $1 billion a year in fees from ratepayers for the U.S. nuclear waste fund, until the government has built a storage site for the spent fuel.

Under a 1982 law, the government was supposed to have started taking away spent fuel from power plants by February 1998, but the Energy Department is still one year away from determining whether the waste could be buried safely at the prescribed site, Yucca Mountain in Nevada.
Under the nuclear waste bill in the House, the government would have to store the nuclear waste above ground at the Nevada Test Site near Yucca Mountain until it is ready to bury the spent fuel.

A substitute bill, expected to be offered Thursday, would also cap utilities' payments into the nuclear waste fund, which an aide to Markey said would jeopardize the whole nuclear waste program because there would not be enough money to build an interim facility and a permanent dump at the same time.
